stem: Ryan is a 14-year-old boy with sudden severe lower abdominal and groin pain. He has a swollen, erythematous, tender right scrotum. Which other finding is most likely on examination?
explanation: This presentation is most consistent with testicular torsion. Typical findings include sudden severe pain, scrotal swelling, and an absent cremasteric reflex. A history of a similar self-limiting episode can suggest intermittent torsion.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Abdominal pain

rationale: A painful swollen hemiscrotum with acute onset abdominal/groin pain in an adolescent is classic for testicular torsion. The absent cremasteric reflex is the most likely associated exam finding.

optionExplanations.A: Prehn’s sign is classically associated with epididymitis, not torsion.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: torsion commonly causes loss of the cremasteric reflex on the affected side.
optionExplanations.D: Torsion is usually unilateral rather than bilateral.
optionExplanations.E: The blue dot sign suggests torsion of a testicular appendage.

source.questionTextHtml: After you have thoroughly examined Ryan’s abdomen and have noted lower abdominal and groin pain, you examine Ryan’s scrotum, even though he blushes. You find a swollen, erythematous, tender right scrotum. Which other finding are you most likely to encounter on examination?

Clinical Scenario 1 - Ryan

You are taking a detailed history from Ryan, a 14 year old boy presenting with acute onset abdominal pain, 8/10 for 2 hours, who can barely walk and has had no vomiting. A few weeks ago there was a similar episode that was self-limiting. There is no history of abdominal trauma and no urinary symptoms.
